question.text: In February 2025 Microsoft announced Majorana 1, a chip it said hosted eight topological qubits, alongside a peer-reviewed Nature paper. What did Nature's own editorial team say the paper did not do?
options: Represent evidence for the presence of Majorana zero modes in the reported devices
Pass peer review, which is why it was published as a preprint instead
Demonstrate that the chip could execute a two-qubit gate
Report the disorder levels in the devices, which the referees had asked for
question.hint: The paper was published and it did demonstrate a real measurement. The caveat is about what that measurement is evidence FOR.

explain.g: The paper was real, peer-reviewed and showed a genuine measurement. What the journal's editors added was a note that the measurement is not evidence the exotic states the whole approach depends on are actually there. That is a third epistemic state, and it is the interesting one: not proven, not disproven, publicly unresolved. Physicists are on the record disagreeing in both directions.
explain.y: The paper demonstrated an interferometric single-shot parity measurement consistent with topological behaviour. Consistent with is not evidence for, and the editorial note said so. Named physicists split publicly: some argued the topological gap protocol gives inconsistent verdicts depending on parameter range, others called the released data noise, while the co-author of the original 2010 proposal stayed engaged and said the devices' disorder needs to improve further before the question is settled experimentally.
explain.r: Microsoft Azure Quantum et al., “Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices,” Nature 638, 651 (2025), with the accompanying editorial note. The field has been burned here before: a 2018 Majorana-conductance paper from a Microsoft-affiliated Delft lab was retracted in March 2021 after a mundane non-topological explanation was shown to produce the same data. None of this makes topological qubits a dead end. It makes the claim unresolved, in public, right now.
